title: RCC RefCert: A Research Toolkit for Structure-Fair Quantum Circuit Complexity
description:
RCC RefCert is an open-source toolkit for studying quantum circuit complexity. Given the parameters of your preparation model, you can compute a rigorous lower bound on optimal quantum circuit complexity from final-state data. Use the target state's exact spectrum or counts collected under a prespecified measurement protocol.

You can model preparations with measurement, feed-forward and reset. In exact diagonal-preserving models, a program that reaches the target within tolerance is provably optimal if its cost matches the lower bound. A density matrix lets you map complexity across the subsystems of a pure or mixed state. Complete outcome counts from a projective measurement give confidence intervals for the complexity it resolves in one state or for the difference in that reading between two states measured the same way. A colleague can independently recompute the analysis from a single bundle.

The toolkit is based on Reference-Contingent Complexity (RCC), introduced by Liu, Tian and Wu in Structure-Fair Quantum Circuit Complexity: An Auditable Information-Theoretic Lower Bound.

Features of reference-contingent complexity

Structural fairness makes circuit complexity comparable across physical settings

Quantum circuit complexity is often measured by the minimum number of gates needed to prepare a target state from a fixed initial state. Counting starts once the inputs are ready, so equal gate counts can conceal different physical costs. For example, one device may supply a pure ancillary qubit, while another must first reset a qubit in a mixed state to obtain one. RCC takes structural fairness as a physical postulate, using the structure reliably supplied by the background as the reference zero point and fixing the available controls and their costs before the target is chosen. It counts only the resources used to generate additional structure and measures them on a common calibrated scale, making quantum circuit complexity comparable across physical settings.

Final-state data give a rigorous lower bound on optimal circuit complexity

With the model, cost rules and required accuracy fixed, optimal quantum circuit complexity is the infimum of the costs of all circuits that successfully prepare the target. Each such circuit must generate the structure the target requires beyond what the reference already supplies. Although this global optimum is often hard to compute directly, RCC certifies an auditable lower bound from final-state data alone, using either the target state's exact spectrum or counts showing that a prespecified outcome is more likely in the target state than in the reference state.

Research tasks

  • Build a finite-control model for RCC certification. Describe your setup in terms of its reference state, available quantum channels and control rules. Once you verify its reference bound, you can use that bound for different targets in the same model.
  • Certify a lower bound on optimal circuit complexity. Rule out circuits below the certified cost for your target and tolerance. Use an exact spectrum or plan a measurement and certify the bound from counts at a prespecified confidence level. In the graph-state example, the same shot budget gives different bounds depending on the measurement settings.
  • Compare preparation strategies. See which programs reach your target within tolerance and what each one costs. In an exact diagonal-preserving model, a successful program is optimal when its cost matches the lower bound. A better program could save at most the gap between that cost and the lower bound. The cooling study finds a six-slot optimum for the full three-qubit target at trace-distance tolerance 1/50.
  • Measure pure-state complexity with window RCC. Subsystem profiles show how complexity is distributed within a pure state and where two states differ, even when their global RCC readings agree. For pure or mixed states, use your own density matrix to separate the contributions of local structure and correlations between subsystems and track both during preparation. Complete histograms from the same projective measurement give a confidence interval for the difference between two states' RCC readings in that classical window.
  • Share a calculation for independent verification. Send a colleague one bundle containing the original inputs and results so they can recompute and verify the calculation independently.
  • Reproduce the paper's reference calculations. Run python -m rcc_refcert reproduce --check to reproduce the bundled cases. Three MATCH results confirm agreement with the frozen expectations, data and report. The paper-to-code map connects the cases to the paper's equations.

Run and share a calculation

With Python 3.10 or newer, install the 0.4.0 source and run the four-qubit reset task in a new working directory.

python -m pip install https://github.com/yeruciwenrou-dotcom/rcc-refcert/archive/6e8878d563a1b204767823800320aa2dd6959e4d.zip
python -m rcc_refcert cost template cyclic-reset > task.json
python -m rcc_refcert cost analyze task.json --bundle task.rccbundle

At the default trace-distance tolerance of 1/10, the result is [5,5] atomic slots. The model rules out shorter programs, and a five-slot program reaches the target with halt included. Change epsilon in task.json to try another tolerance and choose a new bundle filename for the next run. Verify the saved calculation with the following command.

python -m rcc_refcert bundle verify task.rccbundle

New in 0.4.0. Plan a fixed sample size for a preparation-cost threshold and certify a lower bound from target and reference counts, accounting for known binary readout errors. Full outcome histograms give finite-sample intervals for RCC in the measured classical window and for the difference between two states measured there. Import Qiskit readouts from your own runs or check bit order with archived IBM Vigo counts. Explore finite-data studies of a noisy six-qubit cluster state and three-qubit algorithmic cooling, and a half-erasure benchmark with an analytic optimum. Full release notes.

Interpreting the results

Exact diagonal-preserving models can bracket the optimal preparation cost between a rigorous lower bound and the cost of a successful program. For general matrix models, the numerical checks give each candidate's cost and trace distance from the target. Window RCC compares state-side complexity at a fixed reference and control bandwidth. A finite-accuracy lower bound on preparation cost also uses the model parameters and one-shot corrections. The scientific scope explains the quantities and their units.
